specPoints.text: understand the distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary halogenoalkanes

primer.text: Halogenoalkanes are named like addressed envelopes: halogen prefix, numbered position, alphabetical order. This note drills the naming craft across three canonical structures, then classifies primary, secondary and tertiary by counting the alkyl neighbours of the carbon wearing the halogen badge.

lessons.title: Naming the halogenoalkanes
lessons.opening: Halogenoalkanes are alkanes wearing a halogen badge: fluoro, chloro, bromo or iodo prefixes, numbered positions, alphabetical ordering. Three examples - 1-bromopropane, 2-bromopropane, 1-bromo-2-chloropropane - cover the whole naming craft.
keyPoints: The prefixes fluoro, chloro, bromo and iodo mark fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine.
The name is built on the original alkane: CH3CH2CH2Br is 1-bromopropane.
The halogen's position must be numbered: CH3CH(Br)CH3 is 2-bromopropane.
Multiple substituents are listed alphabetically: CH3CH(Cl)CH2Br is 1-bromo-2-chloropropane.

low.restatement: Read the formula, find the longest chain, number from the end that gives the lowest locants, then list halogen prefixes alphabetically with their numbers.
low.analogy: A street address: pick the street (chain), give the house number (locant), list occupants in alphabetical order.
low.examPointer: Alphabetical order ignores the number prefixes - bromo precedes chloro even when chloro carries the lower locant.

medium.restatement: Nomenclature is deterministic: prefix identifies the halogen, locant pins the carbon, alphabetical ordering handles co-substituents. The carbon chain name comes from the parent alkane regardless of which halogen rides it.
medium.analogy: Names are filing labels: colour tag (halogen), shelf number (locant), then alphabetical filing of all tags.
medium.examPointer: Practise all three examples; exam questions recycle 1-bromo-2-chloropropane-style doubles.

check.modelAnswer: 1-bromopropane, bromine on the first carbon of the propane chain.

check.stem: State the four halogen prefixes in nomenclature.
check.modelAnswer: Fluoro, chloro, bromo and iodo, for fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine respectively.

check.stem: Explain why CH3CH(Br)CH3 and CH3CH2CH2Br have different names despite the same molecular formula.
check.modelAnswer: The bromine occupies different carbon positions, so the locants differ, giving positional isomers 2-bromopropane versus 1-bromopropane.

check.stem: A student draws CH3CH2CH(Cl)CH3 and names it 3-chlorobutane. Correct the name.
check.modelAnswer: Numbering from the nearer end gives carbon 2 for the chlorine, so the correct name is 2-chlorobutane.

lessons.title: Primary, secondary and tertiary classification
lessons.opening: One number decides the class: how many alkyl groups hold hands with the halogen-bearing carbon. One makes it primary, two secondary, three tertiary - and skeletal formulae make the count visible.
keyPoints: Halogenoalkanes are classified by the number of alkyl groups attached to the C-X carbon.
A primary halogenoalkane has the halogen on a carbon attached to one other alkyl group.
A secondary halogenoalkane has the halogen on a carbon attached to two other alkyl groups.
A tertiary halogenoalkane has the halogen on a carbon attached to three other alkyl groups.

low.restatement: Count the alkyl neighbours of the carbon carrying the halogen; that count (1, 2 or 3) is the class.
low.analogy: Counting seats at the halogen's dinner table: one companion is primary, two secondary, three tertiary.
low.examPointer: Count alkyl GROUPS, not hydrogen atoms - the C-X carbon's hydrogen count misleads when branching varies.

medium.restatement: The classification is structural, independent of chain length: the halogen-bearing carbon's substitution degree sets the class. Structural, displayed and skeletal formulae all reveal the same count.
medium.analogy: A junction with one, two or three roads meeting: the junction's degree names the class regardless of road length.
medium.examPointer: Practise reading skeletal formulae - examiners hide tertiary centres inside apparently simple structures.

options.explanation: Halogen count is irrelevant to the class.

options.explanation: Chain length does not set the class.

options.explanation: One alkyl neighbour marks the primary class; two mark the secondary.

check.modelAnswer: A halogenoalkane whose halogen-bearing carbon is attached to two other alkyl groups.

check.stem: State how many alkyl groups attach to the C-X carbon in a tertiary halogenoalkane.
Explain why classification depends only on the C-X carbon's neighbours.
check.modelAnswer: The class names the substitution degree of the functional carbon, so only the alkyl groups bonded to that specific carbon count.

check.stem: Classify 1-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane without drawing full formulae.
check.modelAnswer: 1-bromobutane: the C-Br carbon is an end carbon with one alkyl neighbour - primary. 2-bromo-2-methylpropane: the C-Br carbon touches three methyl groups - tertiary.

glossary.definition: An alkane derivative carrying at least one halogen atom bonded to a carbon of the chain.
The number pinning a substituent's position on the parent chain.
A halogenoalkane whose C-X carbon is attached to exactly one other alkyl group.
A halogenoalkane whose C-X carbon is attached to three other alkyl groups.
